dharana.sanskrit_iast: sarvajñaḥ sarvakartā ca vyāpakaḥ parameśvaraḥ | sa evāhaṃ śaivadharmā iti dārḍhyāc chivo bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: 'The supreme Lord is all-knowing, all-doing and all-pervading. I am he, having the qualities of Śiva': through the firmness of this conviction, one becomes Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the dhāraṇā of the first phase of recognition (pratyabhijñā): one is Śiva in essence, masked as an individual (jīva); when the individual intensely recognises its essential reality, the mask falls away and grace (anugraha) operates. Wallis: 'I have Śiva's qualities'.

instruction: Recognise in yourself the qualities of the supreme: knowing, acting and pervading.

method.text: Reflect on the qualities of the supreme: knowing everything, doing everything, present everywhere. Then recognise those same capacities in yourself: you know, you act, your awareness extends. Hold that recognition firmly and rest in it.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 109 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The conviction 'I share the qualities of Śiva: knowing, doing, pervading'
attention.secondary: Steady, firm recognition

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is recognition: the qualities of the whole found, in seed, in oneself.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. This is recognition of essential nature, not a claim to special powers. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: When the Mind Gives Up: The Stillness After an Impasse

title: Unmoving Eyes; Ears and Lower Openings Closed (Classical)
sanskrit: netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ … saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 113: Eyes ‘paralyzed’ (Y88 ~ C1); verse 114: Blocking the ears and hearing the unstruck sound (Y89 ~ A2)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 113 'Dharana 90', verse 114 'Dharana 91', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 89. Not followed.
numbering_variants.two_verses: Singh heads verses 113 and 114 together as one dhāraṇā; Wallis counts them as two yuktis (Y88, Y89).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sampradāyam imam devi śṛṇu samyag vadāmy aham | kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre tathaiva ca | anackam ahalaṃ dhyāyan viśed brahma sanātanam ||
dharana.rendering: (113) O Goddess, listen: I shall tell you this tradition fully. For one whose eyes are held motionless, aloneness-in-freedom (kaivalya) arises at once. (114) Contracting the ears, and the lower opening likewise, meditating on the unstruck sound without vowel or consonant, one enters the eternal brahman.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the unmoving eyes refer to the bhairavī mudrā, eyes open outward without blinking while attention turns to the reality within; he cites Kṣemarāja's Svacchanda Tantra commentary. In 114, the openings of the ears and of the anus and genital are contracted and one meditates on the inner, unstruck sound (anāhata) without vowel or consonant; he relates it to bindu (Śiva) and pure visarga (Śakti). He stresses that kaivalya here is not Sāṃkhya isolation but the world contracted into Śiva. Wallis counts the verses as two yuktis: 'eyes paralyzed' (Y88) and 'blocking the ears and hearing the unstruck sound' (Y89).

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. Do not hold an unblinking gaze, press the ears, or contract the pelvic openings from this door. For gentle related practices, use Door 066 or Door 017.

method.text: Classical method: with the eyes held motionless, aloneness-in-freedom arises at once; contracting the ears and the lower opening, and meditating on the unstruck sound without vowel or consonant, one enters the eternal brahman.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

dharana.rendering: 'For me there is no bondage and no liberation; these are bogeys for the frightened. This world is a reflection in the intellect, like the sun in water.'

instruction: Notice that pleasure and pain come through the senses, and let attention turn back to rest at ease within.

method.text: Notice that every pleasant or unpleasant experience arrives through a sense: seeing, hearing, touch, taste, smell. Without closing anything off, let attention stop reaching out through those doors and turn back. Rest, at ease, in yourself.

dharana.rendering: Everything is revealed by knowing, and the Self is revealed by everything; because their nature is one, knowing and the known are contemplated as one.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'knowing' here stands for the knower; the known is revealed by the knower and the knower by the known. Singh reports a second reading, per Lakshmanjoo: 'knowledge reveals things in the world and the Self is the source of all revelation; since they are not different, the knower is revealed in knowledge'. Wallis's translation follows that reading.

instruction: Notice that what you know and the one who knows reveal each other, and rest in them as one knowing.
